text.p: General Acceptance Corp said Tuesday it entered into a new agreement with its primary lender, providing for a $70.0 million revolving line of credit subject to a maximum advance rate of 78 percent of eligible contracts receivable.
The agreement expires January 1, 1998, and carries an interest rate of one-month LIBOR plus 4.5 percent.
The agreement concludes a nearly 15-month period during which the company operated under default of its prior agreement with the lender, General Acceptance added.
The company said it believes the new agreement gives it sufficient available lines of credit to fund its planned contract acquisition and origination activities throughout 1997.
The company also said it issued $10.0 million in 12.0 percent convertible subordinated notes to an affiliate of Conseco Inc in exchange for cash.

The notes require the payment of interest only, are unsecured and mature on the third anniversary of issuance. The conversion feature of the notes is subject to approval by shareholders at the company's 1997 annual meeting, it added.
If approved, the notes would be convertible into common stock at a conversion price of $3.00 per share. Proceeds were used to reduce borrowings under the revolving line of credit.

General Acceptance said the issuance of the notes to Conseco, along with the credit agreement, will provide it with sufficient liquidity to execute its strategy of building its portfolio of installment sale contracts and opening additional used vehicle dealerships in selected markets.
Conseco also has the right to control one-third of the board of directors and to appoint one person to act in an operations capacity, General Acceptance said.

Also, if Conseco makes a tender offer to all stockholders prior to April 11, 1998, certain principal stockholders of the company may be required to tender a significant portion of shares held by them, General Acceptance added.

The company said it issued $3.3 million in convertible subordinated notes to certain principal stockholders and their relatives in exchange for a 12.0 percent demand notes. Terms of these notes are identical to those issued to Conseco
If Conseco and the others converted their notes, Conseco would own about 32 percent of the total common stock.

The company said it also closed financing operations in several areas and its plans to concentrate the majority of its resources on Indiana, Ohio and Florida. Focusing on these principal markets will increase efficiency, reduce costs and improve its ability to execute its business plan, it added.

In connection with this plan, the company recently completed the sale of an additional $24.7 million of installment sale contracts on a non-recourse basis at 92.7 percent of net principal balance for cash proceeds of $22.9 million. No material gain or loss was recorded.
Proceeds of the sale were used to reduce borrowings. The company said it may sell additonal installment contracts.
